cards.q: A sudden fall in arterial blood pressure is detected first by which receptors?
cards.a: Arterial baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch.
options: Arterial baroreceptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch
Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies
Osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus
Volume receptors in the walls of the atria
cards.explanation: Baroreceptors are stretch endings that fire in proportion to how far the vessel wall is distended, so a fall in pressure drops their firing within a single heartbeat and the medulla answers in seconds. Peripheral chemoreceptors respond to low PO2, high PCO2 and low pH, and they contribute to pressure control only when perfusion gets bad enough to make them ischemic. Osmoreceptors track plasma osmolarity and drive ADH and thirst, a much slower loop. Atrial volume receptors sense filling and matter for long term volume regulation, but they do not carry the fast beat to beat pressure signal.

cards.q: Renin is released into the blood by which cells?
cards.a: Granular cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole.
options: Macula densa cells of the distal tubule
Principal cells of the collecting duct
Granular cells in the wall of the afferent arteriole
Endothelial cells on the surface of the pulmonary capillaries
cards.explanation: Granular cells, also called juxtaglomerular cells, sit in the afferent arteriole wall and release renin when perfusion pressure falls, when sympathetic drive rises, or when the macula densa reports low NaCl delivery. The macula densa is the sensor that signals them, not the source of the hormone. Principal cells are targets further downstream, responding to aldosterone and ADH. Pulmonary capillary endothelium carries ACE, which converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II, a later step in the same pathway.

cards.q: What stimulus triggers release of atrial natriuretic peptide?
cards.a: Stretch of the atrial wall by an increased blood volume.
options: A fall in plasma sodium concentration
Stretch of the atrial wall by an increased blood volume
A rise in plasma potassium concentration
A fall in perfusion pressure sensed at the afferent arteriole
cards.explanation: ANP is stored in atrial myocytes and released when a volume load stretches the atria, after which it promotes Na+ and water excretion and opposes the renin pathway. A fall in perfusion pressure at the afferent arteriole is the trigger for renin, the arm that works in the opposite direction. A rise in plasma K+ stimulates aldosterone directly from the adrenal cortex. Plasma Na+ concentration is defended mainly by ADH and thirst rather than by ANP release.

cards.q: Which chemical buffer system carries most of the buffering capacity of extracellular fluid?
cards.a: The bicarbonate and carbonic acid system.
options: The phosphate buffer system
The hemoglobin buffer inside red cells
The plasma protein buffer system
The bicarbonate and carbonic acid system
cards.explanation: Bicarbonate is present in high concentration and works as an open system: the lung sets PCO2 and the kidney sets HCO3-, so the buffer can be regenerated rather than used up. Phosphate is a strong buffer where its concentration is high, which is inside cells and in the urine, not in plasma. Hemoglobin buffers a great deal of H+, but it is inside the red cell rather than in extracellular fluid proper. Plasma proteins do buffer, but their concentration in ECF is far below that of bicarbonate.

cards.q: In metabolic acidosis, which system compensates first and over what time scale?
cards.a: The respiratory system, within minutes.
options: The kidney, within minutes
The respiratory system, over two to three days
The kidney, within a few heartbeats
The respiratory system, within minutes
cards.explanation: Falling pH excites central and peripheral chemoreceptors, ventilation rises, CO2 is blown off, and pH moves back toward normal within minutes. The kidney also compensates, excreting H+ and generating new HCO3-, but that response needs hours to days to develop. Nothing in acid-base compensation acts on a beat to beat time scale; that speed belongs to the baroreflex, which is neural rather than chemical.

cards.q: In acid-base physiology, what does the term compensation mean?
cards.a: A response by the system that did not cause the problem, shifting pH toward normal.
options: Return of the primary disturbance itself to its normal value by the same system
A response by the system that did not cause the problem, shifting pH toward normal
A secondary change that drives pH further away from the normal range
Restoration of arterial pH exactly to 7.40 once the response is complete
cards.explanation: Compensation means the other system answers: the lung adjusts PCO2 for a metabolic problem, and the kidney adjusts HCO3- for a respiratory one. Fixing the primary problem itself is correction, a different word worth keeping separate. Compensation moves pH toward normal but almost never all the way to 7.40, which is a useful clue when reading blood gas values. A change that worsens pH is not compensation at all.

cards.q: What is the main renal action of antidiuretic hormone?
cards.a: It puts water channels in the collecting duct so water is reabsorbed.
options: It drives Na+ reabsorption in the distal nephron in exchange for K+
It constricts the efferent arteriole to raise filtration pressure
It puts water channels in the collecting duct so water is reabsorbed
It blocks distal Na+ reabsorption and raises the Na+ in the urine
cards.explanation: ADH moves aquaporin-2 into the apical membrane of collecting duct cells, so water follows the medullary osmotic gradient out of the tubule and the urine is concentrated. Trading Na+ for K+ in the distal nephron is aldosterone's action. Constricting the efferent arteriole is angiotensin II. Blocking distal Na+ reabsorption to raise urinary Na+ describes ANP, the hormone that opposes this whole arm.

cards.q: A fall in arterial PO2 is sensed by which receptors?
cards.a: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies.
options: Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid and aortic bodies
Central chemoreceptors on the ventral surface of the medulla
Stretch receptors in the airway walls
Juxtacapillary receptors in the alveolar wall
cards.explanation: Only the carotid and aortic bodies respond to arterial PO2, and they fire hard once PO2 drops below roughly 60 mmHg. Central chemoreceptors read the pH of brain extracellular fluid, which tracks arterial PCO2, and they are blind to oxygen. Airway stretch receptors drive the Hering-Breuer inflation reflex, ending an inspiration that goes too far. Juxtacapillary receptors respond to engorgement of the alveolar interstitium and produce rapid shallow breathing.

cards.q: A person loses 700 mL of blood over a few minutes. What happens to carotid sinus baroreceptor firing?
cards.a: It falls, because the vessel wall is stretched less.
options: It falls, because the vessel wall is stretched less
It rises, because the heart is beating faster
It rises, because blood shifts centrally and stretches the sinus
It is unchanged, because these endings sense plasma osmolarity
cards.explanation: Baroreceptors report wall stretch, so a smaller volume at a lower pressure means fewer action potentials travelling up the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves. The medulla reads that drop as low pressure and raises sympathetic outflow, which is why heart rate goes up. Heart rate does not drive baroreceptor firing; the reflex runs the other way, from sensor to effector. Osmolarity is the business of hypothalamic osmoreceptors, not of these endings.

cards.q: During the sympathetic response to hemorrhage, what does venoconstriction accomplish?
cards.a: It shifts stored blood toward the heart and raises preload.
options: It raises total peripheral resistance and so raises afterload
It lowers venous compliance so less blood reaches the right atrium
It shifts stored blood toward the heart and raises preload
It raises capillary hydrostatic pressure and speeds up filtration
cards.explanation: About two thirds of the blood volume sits in veins, so squeezing them pushes volume centrally, raising venous return, end diastolic volume, and stroke volume through the Frank-Starling mechanism. Raising resistance and afterload is what arteriolar constriction does, a different vessel and a different purpose. Lower venous compliance moves blood toward the heart, not away from it. Capillary hydrostatic pressure actually falls in hemorrhage, which pulls interstitial fluid into the plasma and helps refill it.

cards.q: A frightened person hyperventilates for several minutes. What happens to arterial PCO2 and pH?
cards.a: PCO2 falls and pH rises.
options: PCO2 falls and pH falls
PCO2 falls and pH rises
PCO2 rises and pH falls
PCO2 rises and pH rises
cards.explanation: Blowing off CO2 faster than metabolism makes it lowers PCO2, which pulls the CO2 and water reaction backward and removes H+, so pH rises. That is respiratory alkalosis. Rising PCO2 with falling pH is the opposite disturbance, respiratory acidosis, and it comes from hypoventilation. When the lung is the source of the problem, PCO2 and pH always move in opposite directions.

cards.q: Prolonged watery diarrhea loses large amounts of bicarbonate from the gut. Which disturbance results?
cards.a: Metabolic acidosis.
options: Metabolic alkalosis
Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory alkalosis
Metabolic acidosis
cards.explanation: Losing HCO3- leaves relatively more H+ in the extracellular fluid, so pH falls and measured plasma HCO3- is low, which is metabolic acidosis. The loss did not happen through the lung, so the problem is not respiratory. Vomiting is the mirror case: gastric HCl leaves the body and metabolic alkalosis follows. Respiratory disturbances always start with a change in ventilation that moves PCO2 first.

cards.q: A hiker sweats for hours without drinking and plasma osmolarity rises from 290 to 302 mOsm/L. Which response comes first?
cards.a: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors fire more and ADH release rises.
options: Atrial stretch receptors fire more and ANP release rises
Granular cells stop releasing renin as filtered Na+ climbs
Aldosterone falls and more Na+ appears in the urine
Hypothalamic osmoreceptors fire more and ADH release rises
cards.explanation: Osmoreceptors respond to shifts of only one or two percent in osmolarity, so ADH rises early and the kidney holds on to water. ANP release needs atrial stretch, which needs a volume load, the opposite of what dehydration produces. Renin rises rather than stops in dehydration, because renal perfusion and distal Na+ delivery both fall. Aldosterone rises for the same reason, conserving Na+ instead of dumping it in the urine.

cards.q: Renal perfusion pressure falls. Angiotensin II constricts which vessel to protect glomerular filtration rate?
cards.a: The efferent arteriole.
options: The afferent arteriole
The efferent arteriole
The peritubular capillary
The vasa recta
cards.explanation: Constricting downstream of the glomerulus dams up pressure inside the glomerular capillary and holds filtration up even though total renal flow has dropped. Constricting the afferent arteriole would do the reverse, lowering glomerular pressure and dropping GFR further. The peritubular capillaries and the vasa recta lie beyond the efferent arteriole and carry blood away from the glomerulus, so narrowing them cannot raise filtration pressure.

cards.q: Heart rate rises from 70 to 100 beats per minute while stroke volume stays at 70 mL. What is the new cardiac output?
cards.a: 7.0 L/min.
options: 4.9 L/min
5.6 L/min
7.0 L/min
10.0 L/min
cards.explanation: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume, so 100 beats per minute times 70 mL per beat gives 7000 mL/min, which is 7.0 L/min. 4.9 L/min is the resting value, before the rate changed. 5.6 L/min comes from using a rate of 80 by mistake. 10.0 L/min would need a stroke volume near 100 mL as well as the faster rate.

cards.q: A trauma patient loses about one liter of blood. In what order do the compensations take effect?
cards.a: Baroreflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction, then ADH and thirst, then aldosterone driven Na+ retention.
options: Baroreflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction, then ADH and thirst, then aldosterone driven Na+ retention
ADH and thirst, then baroreflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction, then aldosterone driven Na+ retention
Aldosterone driven Na+ retention, then ADH and thirst, then baroreflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction
Baroreflex tachycardia and vasoconstriction, then aldosterone driven Na+ retention, then a fall in ADH
cards.explanation: The neural reflex is the only response fast enough to act within seconds, so it always comes first and defends pressure while everything else is still getting started. ADH rises within minutes as low pressure and rising angiotensin II reach the hypothalamus and posterior pituitary. Aldosterone driven Na+ retention and the real rebuilding of volume take hours. Any order that puts a hormone ahead of the reflex ignores the difference between nerve conduction and hormone synthesis and transport, and ADH must rise, not fall, when volume is low.

cards.q: A patient vomits repeatedly for two days, losing gastric HCl. Which arterial values fit that disturbance plus its expected compensation?
cards.a: pH 7.50, HCO3- 34 mEq/L, PCO2 46 mmHg.
options: pH 7.50, HCO3- 34 mEq/L, PCO2 46 mmHg
pH 7.28, HCO3- 16 mEq/L, PCO2 30 mmHg
pH 7.50, HCO3- 23 mEq/L, PCO2 30 mmHg
pH 7.30, HCO3- 30 mEq/L, PCO2 60 mmHg
cards.explanation: Losing H+ in vomit leaves excess HCO3- behind, so pH and HCO3- both rise, which is metabolic alkalosis. The lung compensates by slowing ventilation and holding on to CO2, so PCO2 climbs above 40 mmHg. Low pH with a low HCO3- and a low PCO2 is metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation, the mirror image of this case. High pH with a normal HCO3- and a low PCO2 is a primary respiratory alkalosis. Low pH with a high PCO2 and a high HCO3- is respiratory acidosis with renal compensation.

cards.q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis is making ketoacids and spilling glucose into the urine. Tracing this through the lung and kidney, which pair of findings follows?
cards.a: Deep rapid breathing with a low PCO2, and volume depletion from an osmotic diuresis.
options: Slow shallow breathing with a high PCO2, and volume depletion from an osmotic diuresis
Deep rapid breathing with a low PCO2, and volume expansion from water retention
Deep rapid breathing with a low PCO2, and volume depletion from an osmotic diuresis
Normal breathing with a normal PCO2, and volume depletion from a fall in ADH
cards.explanation: Ketoacids drive pH down, chemoreceptors respond with the deep rapid breathing named after Kussmaul, and PCO2 falls as respiratory compensation. At the same time filtered glucose exceeds the tubular transport maximum, stays in the tubule and holds water with it, so urine volume climbs and extracellular volume falls. Hypoventilation would raise PCO2 and worsen the acidosis rather than compensate for it. Volume cannot expand while an osmotic diuresis is running, and ADH rises rather than falls once volume drops.

cards.q: After three days at 4000 meters, a lowlander shows which set of changes?
cards.a: Higher ventilation, arterial pH back near normal, and a lower plasma HCO3-.
options: Higher ventilation, arterial pH clearly alkaline, and a raised plasma HCO3-
Higher ventilation, arterial pH back near normal, and a lower plasma HCO3-
Lower ventilation, arterial pH clearly acidic, and a raised plasma HCO3-
Unchanged ventilation, arterial pH back near normal, and a lower plasma HCO3-
cards.explanation: Low inspired PO2 excites the peripheral chemoreceptors, ventilation rises and PCO2 falls, which on the first day gives a respiratory alkalosis. Over the next two days the kidney excretes HCO3-, so plasma HCO3- falls and pH returns toward normal while ventilation stays high. A raised HCO3- would be renal compensation for an acidosis, the wrong direction here. Ventilation cannot be unchanged, because the hypoxic drive is what starts the whole sequence.

cards.q: Which fuel supplies ATP to skeletal muscle during the first several seconds of hard contraction?
cards.a: Creatine phosphate, which hands its phosphate to ADP.
options: Glucose taken through anaerobic glycolysis to lactate
Fatty acids oxidized inside the mitochondria
Muscle glycogen fed into oxidative phosphorylation
Creatine phosphate, which hands its phosphate to ADP
cards.explanation: Creatine phosphate is already sitting in the fiber and needs a single enzyme step, so it buffers ATP for roughly the first ten seconds of work. Anaerobic glycolysis takes over for the next minute or two, at the cost of lactate accumulation. Fatty acid oxidation dominates at rest and in prolonged moderate exercise but is slow to ramp up. Glycogen fed to oxidative phosphorylation supports steady sustained work, not the first few contractions.

cards.q: At the onset of exercise heart rate rises within one or two beats. Which change accounts for that speed?
cards.a: Withdrawal of parasympathetic tone from the SA node.
options: Sympathetic release of norepinephrine at the SA node
Circulating epinephrine arriving from the adrenal medulla
Increased venous return stretching the SA node
Withdrawal of parasympathetic tone from the SA node
cards.explanation: Vagal traffic to the SA node is heavy at rest and acetylcholine is broken down in milliseconds, so lifting that brake raises rate almost at once. Sympathetic norepinephrine works through a second messenger cascade and takes several seconds to build its effect. Adrenal epinephrine is slower still, because it has to travel in the blood to reach the node. Stretch of the SA node does raise rate a little through the Bainbridge reflex, but the effect is small next to vagal withdrawal.

cards.q: Which local changes in a contracting muscle produce active hyperemia?
cards.a: Rising interstitial K+, adenosine, CO2 and H+.
options: Rising interstitial Ca2+, Na+ and HCO3-
Rising interstitial K+, adenosine, CO2 and H+
Falling interstitial K+ together with a rising PO2
Rising circulating angiotensin II and vasopressin
cards.explanation: Working fibers lose K+ with every action potential and make adenosine, CO2 and H+, all of which relax arteriolar smooth muscle so flow rises to match demand. Interstitial oxygen falls during exercise rather than rising, and that fall is itself part of the dilator signal. Ca2+, Na+ and HCO3- do not accumulate in the interstitium in step with metabolic rate. Angiotensin II and vasopressin are circulating constrictors, the opposite of a local dilator signal.

cards.q: What happens to total peripheral resistance during moderate whole body exercise?
cards.a: It falls, because muscle arterioles dilate across a very large bed.
options: It rises, because sympathetic drive to arterioles increases
It is unchanged, because dilation and constriction cancel each other out
It falls, because muscle arterioles dilate across a very large bed
It falls, because mean arterial pressure drops below rest
cards.explanation: Skeletal muscle is such a large fraction of body mass that dilation there dominates the sum of all the parallel beds, and total resistance falls even while the kidney and gut are constricted. Sympathetic drive does rise, but local metabolites override it inside the working muscle. Mean arterial pressure rises modestly in exercise rather than falling, because cardiac output rises more than resistance falls. Nothing forces dilation and constriction to cancel; the muscle bed simply wins.

cards.q: What happens to blood flow through the kidneys and the gut during moderate exercise?
cards.a: It falls, because sympathetic vasoconstriction narrows those beds.
options: It falls, because sympathetic vasoconstriction narrows those beds
It rises, in proportion to the rise in cardiac output
It rises, because circulating epinephrine dilates them
It is unchanged, because renal autoregulation holds their flow constant
cards.explanation: Sympathetic outflow constricts renal and splanchnic arterioles, so those beds take a smaller share of a larger cardiac output and their absolute flow drops. That redistribution is exactly what lets muscle flow rise many times over. Renal autoregulation stabilizes flow across a range of pressures but is overridden by strong sympathetic drive. Epinephrine acts on beta 2 receptors in muscle and liver vessels, not to protect gut flow during exercise.

cards.q: In a healthy person doing moderate steady exercise, what happens to arterial PCO2?
cards.a: It stays close to its resting value.
options: It stays close to its resting value
It rises steadily as CO2 production increases
It falls steadily through the whole exercise bout
It rises at first and then drops below resting
cards.explanation: Alveolar ventilation rises almost exactly in step with CO2 production, so arterial PCO2 is held near 40 mmHg. That match is the point: ventilation in moderate exercise is driven by feedforward signals and muscle afferents rather than by a rising PCO2. PCO2 does begin to fall once work goes above the lactate threshold, because ventilation then climbs out of proportion. A steady rise in PCO2 would mean ventilation was failing to keep up.

cards.q: Which pair of hormonal changes supports hepatic glucose output during prolonged exercise?
cards.a: Insulin falls and glucagon rises.
options: Insulin rises and glucagon falls
Insulin rises and cortisol falls
Insulin falls and glucagon rises
Insulin falls and aldosterone rises
cards.explanation: Falling insulin releases the brake on glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, and rising glucagon actively drives them, so the liver can supply glucose while muscle is pulling it out of the blood. Insulin rising during exercise would push glucose into storage at exactly the wrong moment. Cortisol rises in prolonged exercise rather than falling, adding to fuel mobilization. Aldosterone does rise with exercise, but its job is Na+ retention, not fuel supply.

cards.q: During dynamic exercise such as jogging, what happens to systolic and diastolic blood pressure?
cards.a: Systolic rises substantially while diastolic changes little.
options: Systolic and diastolic both rise substantially
Systolic rises substantially while diastolic changes little
Systolic changes little while the diastolic rises substantially
Systolic rises while diastolic drops below 40 mmHg
cards.explanation: A bigger, faster stroke volume ejected into the aorta raises systolic pressure, while dilated muscle beds let blood run off quickly during diastole so diastolic pressure stays near rest or dips slightly. Pulse pressure therefore widens, which is a normal exercise finding. A large rise in both would suggest resistance was climbing, which is what static or isometric work does. Diastolic pressure does not normally collapse to very low values in healthy dynamic exercise.

cards.q: At rest a person has a cardiac output of 5 L/min and consumes 250 mL of oxygen per minute. What is the arteriovenous oxygen difference?
cards.a: 50 mL of O2 per liter of blood.
options: 25 mL of O2 per liter of blood
125 mL of O2 per liter of blood
200 mL of O2 per liter of blood
50 mL of O2 per liter of blood
cards.explanation: The Fick relation says oxygen consumption equals cardiac output times the arteriovenous oxygen difference, so 250 mL/min divided by 5 L/min gives 50 mL per liter. 200 mL per liter is the oxygen content of arterial blood, not the amount removed by the tissues. 125 mL per liter is closer to the extraction seen in heavy exercise. 25 mL per liter would mean the tissues took only half of what they actually consume.

cards.q: During upright exercise stroke volume rises. What is the main reason?
cards.a: Greater venous return raises end diastolic volume.
options: Greater afterload from a rising arterial pressure
Shorter filling time as heart rate climbs
Reduced contractility at the higher heart rate
Greater venous return raises end diastolic volume
cards.explanation: The skeletal muscle pump, deeper breathing and venoconstriction all push blood back to the heart, so preload rises and the Frank-Starling mechanism raises stroke volume, with sympathetic contractility adding to it. Rising afterload opposes ejection and would lower stroke volume if nothing else changed. Filling time does shorten at high rates, which is why stroke volume plateaus, but that limits the rise rather than causing it. Contractility increases during exercise rather than falling.

cards.q: Cardiac output rises from 5 to 20 L/min while mean arterial pressure goes only from 90 to 105 mmHg. What happened to total peripheral resistance?
cards.a: It fell to roughly a third of its resting value.
options: It rose in proportion to the rise in cardiac output
It fell to roughly a third of its resting value
It stayed the same, since pressure did rise a little
It fell slightly, by about ten percent
cards.explanation: Mean arterial pressure equals cardiac output times total peripheral resistance, so if flow quadruples and pressure rises by only about a sixth, resistance has to fall to about a third of what it was. Resistance rising would have driven pressure far above 105 mmHg. Unchanged resistance with four times the flow would have roughly quadrupled the pressure. A ten percent fall is nowhere near enough to absorb a fourfold change in flow.

cards.q: How does rhythmic contraction of the leg muscles affect the circulation during walking?
cards.a: It squeezes the deep veins and drives blood toward the heart.
options: It compresses arteries and raises flow into the muscle
It raises venous compliance so blood pools in the legs
It squeezes the deep veins and drives blood toward the heart
It holds the venous valves shut so blood stays in the calf
cards.explanation: Each contraction compresses the deep veins, and because the valves open only toward the heart the blood can move in one direction, so venous return and preload rise. Arterial compression during a contraction briefly reduces inflow; muscle flow actually peaks between contractions. Pooling in the legs is what happens when this pump is absent, as in quiet standing. Valves opening and closing in turn is what makes the pump work, not a trap that holds blood in place.

cards.q: A runner sweats heavily for 90 minutes without drinking. What happens to plasma volume and to ADH release?
cards.a: Plasma volume falls and ADH release rises.
options: Plasma volume falls and ADH release rises
Plasma volume falls and ADH release drops
Plasma volume rises and ADH release rises
Plasma volume rises and ADH release drops
cards.explanation: Sweat is hypotonic compared with plasma, so heavy sweating removes proportionally more water than solute: volume falls and osmolarity rises, and both signals stimulate ADH. The kidney then conserves water and urine volume falls. ADH dropping would waste water at exactly the wrong moment and is what happens after drinking instead. Plasma volume cannot rise while fluid leaves the body unreplaced.

cards.q: Blood arriving in exercising muscle meets a lower pH, a higher PCO2 and a higher temperature. What happens to the oxyhemoglobin curve?
cards.a: It shifts right, so more oxygen is unloaded at a given PO2.
options: It shifts right, so more oxygen is unloaded at a given PO2
It shifts left, so more oxygen is unloaded at a given PO2
It shifts right, so hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly
It shifts left, so hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly
cards.explanation: Acid, CO2, heat and 2,3-BPG all lower hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, the Bohr effect, and the curve moves right so oxygen comes off where the tissue needs it. A right shift and tighter binding cannot go together, since right means looser binding by definition. A left shift means tighter binding, which favors loading in the lung and is what you see in the fetus or in a hypothermic tissue.

cards.q: Above the lactate threshold, ventilation climbs out of proportion to oxygen consumption. What accounts for the extra ventilation?
cards.a: Bicarbonate buffering of lactic acid makes additional CO2.
options: Arterial PO2 drops far enough to excite the chemoreceptors
Rising body temperature acts on the central chemoreceptors
Bicarbonate buffering of lactic acid makes additional CO2
Muscle stretch receptors fire more as contraction force rises
cards.explanation: HCO3- buffers the H+ from lactic acid, and that reaction releases CO2 beyond what metabolism alone produces, so ventilation climbs and arterial PCO2 starts to fall. Arterial PO2 stays well defended in healthy people even at heavy work, so a hypoxic drive is not the trigger. Temperature adds a little to exercise ventilation but does not produce the sharp break seen at threshold. Muscle afferents help drive ventilation from the very start rather than appearing only above threshold.

cards.q: In the first 30 seconds of moderate exercise, which sequence correctly orders the events that raise oxygen delivery to working muscle?
cards.a: Central command withdraws vagal tone, cardiac output rises, then local metabolites dilate muscle arterioles.
options: Local metabolites dilate the muscle arterioles, arterial pressure falls, and only after that does heart rate rise
Central command withdraws vagal tone, cardiac output rises, then local metabolites dilate muscle arterioles
Adrenal epinephrine rises, muscle arterioles dilate, and only then is vagal tone withdrawn
Arterial PO2 falls, peripheral chemoreceptors fire, and ventilation rises before any cardiac change
cards.explanation: Signals descending from the motor cortex reach the medulla at the same instant the muscles are told to contract, so vagal withdrawal and a higher heart rate happen almost immediately, and local metabolic dilation builds over the seconds that follow as the fibers work. Adrenal epinephrine is slower, since it must be carried in the blood. Arterial pressure rises rather than falls at the onset of exercise. Arterial PO2 is well maintained in moderate exercise, so a hypoxic trigger has no part in this sequence.

cards.q: A cyclist rides for two hours in the heat without drinking. Late in the ride, which combination is expected?
cards.a: Falling stroke volume with a rising heart rate, and a small volume of concentrated urine.
options: Rising stroke volume with a falling heart rate, and a large volume of dilute urine
Falling stroke volume with a rising heart rate, and a large volume of dilute urine
Unchanged stroke volume and unchanged heart rate, with a small volume of concentrated urine
Falling stroke volume with a rising heart rate, and a small volume of concentrated urine
cards.explanation: Sweat loss plus skin vasodilation pulls volume out of the central circulation, so preload and stroke volume drift down while heart rate climbs to defend cardiac output, a pattern called cardiovascular drift. At the same time ADH and aldosterone rise, so the kidney holds water and salt and the urine is scant and concentrated. Large dilute urine would mean ADH had been suppressed, which follows drinking rather than dehydration. Heart rate cannot stay flat while stroke volume falls if cardiac output is being held up.

cards.q: At steady state a subject consumes 3.0 L of oxygen per minute with a cardiac output of 20 L/min. If arterial oxygen content is 200 mL per liter, what is the mixed venous oxygen content?
cards.a: 50 mL of O2 per liter.
options: 150 mL of O2 per liter
100 mL of O2 per liter
20 mL of O2 per liter
50 mL of O2 per liter
cards.explanation: By the Fick principle the arteriovenous difference is 3000 mL/min divided by 20 L/min, which is 150 mL per liter, so venous content is 200 minus 150, or 50 mL per liter. Choosing 150 mL per liter reports the difference itself rather than what is left in venous blood. 100 mL per liter is close to resting mixed venous blood, where extraction is far lower. Whole body venous blood never falls to 20 mL per liter, since not every tissue extracts at the rate working muscle does.

cards.q: Suppose local metabolic vasodilation in working muscle were blocked while sympathetic constrictor drive still rose. What would happen during exercise?
cards.a: Muscle blood flow would fail to rise, and extraction alone could not meet demand.
options: Muscle blood flow would rise normally, since cardiac output still increases
Muscle blood flow would fail to rise, and extraction alone could not meet demand
Muscle blood flow would rise even more, since sympathetic drive dilates muscle
Muscle blood flow would fall and arterial pressure would fall along with it
cards.explanation: In normal exercise local metabolites override sympathetic constriction inside the working muscle, which is called functional sympatholysis; take that away and the constrictor signal wins, so the arterioles stay narrow. A larger cardiac output cannot force flow into a bed that has not dilated, because flow through any bed depends on the resistance of that bed. Sympathetic alpha receptor activity constricts muscle arterioles rather than dilating them. Arterial pressure would rise rather than fall, since total peripheral resistance would stay high.

cards.q: In a drawing of a negative feedback loop, what is the correct order of the labeled boxes?
cards.a: Stimulus, sensor, integrating center, effector, response.
options: Stimulus, effector, integrating center, sensor, response
Sensor, stimulus, effector, integrating center, response
Stimulus, sensor, integrating center, effector, response
Stimulus, integrating center, sensor, effector, response
cards.explanation: The pathway runs from the change itself, to a sensor that detects it, along an afferent path to an integrating center that compares the value with a set point, then along an efferent path to an effector that produces the response. Putting the effector before the integrating center takes away the step where the decision is made. Starting with the sensor leaves it nothing to detect. The sensor must come before the integrating center, because the center can only act on what the sensor sends it.

cards.q: On a homeostatic pathway diagram, what does the box labeled integrating center do?
cards.a: It compares the sensed value with the set point and decides the output.
options: It compares the sensed value with the set point and decides the output
It detects the change in the regulated variable and encodes it as a signal
It carries out the change that opposes the original stimulus
It carries the signal from the sensor onward to the effector
cards.explanation: The integrating center, usually a region of the central nervous system or an endocrine cell, holds the set point and issues the command. Detecting and encoding the change is the sensor's job, one box upstream. Carrying out the change belongs to the effector, one box downstream. Carrying the signal is the afferent or efferent pathway, which on a diagram is an arrow rather than a box.

cards.q: In a negative feedback diagram, what must the arrow returning from the response to the stimulus show?
cards.a: That the response reduces the original stimulus.
options: That the response reduces the original stimulus
That the response increases the original stimulus
That the response leaves the original stimulus unchanged
That the sensor reports the response to the integrating center
cards.explanation: Negative feedback means the output feeds back to shut off its own trigger, so the return arrow has to carry a minus sign or the word decreases. An arrow that increases the stimulus describes positive feedback, as in oxytocin during labor. An arrow with no effect describes an open loop, which cannot regulate anything. The path from sensor to integrating center is the afferent limb, drawn earlier in the loop rather than at its close.

cards.q: In a drawn homeostatic loop, where does the set point belong?
cards.a: With the integrating center, as the value it compares against.
options: With the sensor, as the value it is able to detect
With the effector, as the level of output it can produce
With the integrating center, as the value it compares against
With the response, as the value the variable finally reaches
cards.explanation: The set point is a reference held by the integrating center, and the error signal is the difference between the sensed value and that reference. Sensors report values; they do not hold references to compare against. Effectors act on commands, and their maximum output has nothing to do with the set point. The value actually reached is the regulated variable, which oscillates around the set point rather than defining it.

cards.q: What distinguishes a positive feedback diagram from a negative feedback diagram?
cards.a: The return arrow amplifies the stimulus, and an outside event ends the loop.
options: The return arrow reduces the stimulus, and the loop settles at a set point
The return arrow amplifies the stimulus, and an outside event ends the loop
The loop has no sensor, so nothing detects the regulated variable
The loop has two integrating centers instead of one
cards.explanation: In positive feedback the response drives the stimulus harder, so the cycle runs away until something outside the loop stops it, the way birth ends the oxytocin loop and channel inactivation ends the action potential upstroke. A return arrow that reduces the stimulus is precisely the negative feedback case. Positive feedback loops still contain sensors and integrating centers; what changes is the sign of the return arrow, not the number of parts.

cards.q: A student is drawing the baroreceptor reflex. What belongs in the sensor box?
cards.a: Stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch.
options: The cardiovascular center in the medulla oblongata
The SA node and the ventricular myocardium
The granular cells of the afferent arteriole
Stretch receptors in the carotid sinus and aortic arch
cards.explanation: The reflex begins at stretch sensitive nerve endings in the walls of the carotid sinus and aortic arch, which report arterial pressure moment to moment. The medullary cardiovascular center is the integrating center in this loop, not the sensor. The SA node and the myocardium are effectors, changing rate and force on command. Granular cells belong to the renal pathway for long term volume regulation, a slower loop that deserves its own diagram.

cards.q: In a drawing of a hypothalamic and anterior pituitary axis, what are the three signaling levels in order?
cards.a: Hypothalamic releasing hormone, anterior pituitary tropic hormone, target gland hormone.
options: Anterior pituitary tropic hormone, hypothalamic releasing hormone, target gland hormone
Target gland hormone, hypothalamic releasing hormone, anterior pituitary tropic hormone
Hypothalamic releasing hormone, target gland hormone, anterior pituitary tropic hormone
Hypothalamic releasing hormone, anterior pituitary tropic hormone, target gland hormone
cards.explanation: The hypothalamus sends a releasing hormone down the portal vessels, the anterior pituitary answers with a tropic hormone in the general circulation, and the target gland releases the final hormone. That final hormone then feeds back on both levels above it, which is the arrow students most often leave off the page. Any order that puts the pituitary or the target gland first reverses the direction of the portal blood flow and of the feedback.

cards.q: On a physiology diagram, what marks an arrow as feedforward rather than feedback?
cards.a: It acts on an early cue, before the regulated variable has changed.
options: It acts only after the regulated variable has already begun to change
It acts on an early cue, before the regulated variable has changed
It always increases the stimulus that set the pathway going
It links two effectors without passing an integrating center
cards.explanation: Feedforward control acts on an advance cue, such as the sight of food raising insulin secretion or central command raising heart rate the instant exercise begins, before the variable has moved at all. Feedback by definition waits for the variable to change and then responds. Amplifying the stimulus describes positive feedback, which is a separate distinction about the sign of a loop. Feedforward pathways still run through an integrating center.

cards.q: A student's thermoregulation diagram shows core temperature rising, then an arrow to skin arterioles labeled constrict. What correction is needed?
cards.a: The arrow should read dilate, so heat can escape at the skin.
options: The arrow is right, because constriction increases heat loss
The arrow should point to skeletal muscle and read shiver
The arrow should read dilate, so heat can escape at the skin
The arrow should be deleted, since skin vessels are not effectors
cards.explanation: A rising core temperature calls for heat loss, and cutaneous vasodilation brings warm blood to the surface where it can radiate heat away. Constriction conserves heat and belongs on the cold side of the same diagram. Shivering is also a cold response, generating heat rather than losing it. Skin arterioles are among the most important effectors in thermoregulation, so deleting them would gut the loop.

cards.q: A student draws blood glucose rising, beta cells releasing insulin, then an arrow to the liver labeled glycogenolysis. What is wrong?
cards.a: Insulin builds glycogen, so the arrow should read glycogenesis.
options: Insulin builds glycogen, so the arrow should read glycogenesis
Insulin comes from alpha cells, so the cell label is wrong
The arrow should point to the pancreas rather than the liver
The arrow is right, but the stimulus should be a fall in glucose
cards.explanation: Insulin is the storage signal, so after a meal the liver takes up glucose and builds glycogen. Glycogenolysis is glucagon's effect and belongs on the low glucose arm of the same diagram, which is the confusion this card is built around. Beta cells are correctly named as the insulin source; alpha cells make glucagon. The liver is the right target, and a rise in glucose is the right stimulus for insulin.

cards.q: A student's baroreflex sketch starts with blood pressure falling and labels baroreceptor firing as increasing. What should it say?
cards.a: Firing decreases, because less stretch means fewer action potentials.
options: Firing decreases, because less stretch means fewer action potentials
Firing increases, because the reflex must raise sympathetic output
Firing is unchanged, because these endings adapt within a heartbeat
Firing decreases, because these endings sense a fall in blood oxygen
cards.explanation: Baroreceptors are stretch sensors, so a lower pressure stretches the wall less and afferent firing falls; the medulla reads that drop and raises sympathetic outflow. The error in the sketch is matching sensor firing to the direction of the reflex output instead of to the direction of the stimulus. These endings do adapt over days of sustained pressure change, but not within a single beat. Oxygen is the business of chemoreceptors, not baroreceptors.

cards.q: In an ADH pathway drawing, osmolarity rises, ADH is released, and the arrow from the collecting duct reads urine volume increases. What correction is needed?
cards.a: Urine volume decreases, because ADH makes the duct permeable to water.
options: Urine volume increases, because ADH adds Na+ to the filtrate
Urine volume decreases, because ADH lowers the glomerular filtration rate
Urine volume decreases, because ADH makes the duct permeable to water
Urine volume is unchanged, because ADH acts only on thirst
cards.explanation: ADH inserts aquaporin-2 channels so water leaves the collecting duct for the hyperosmotic medulla, giving a small volume of concentrated urine, and that retained water is what pulls osmolarity back toward normal. ADH does not work by changing the filtration rate; its action is on reabsorption further downstream. It does not add Na+ to the filtrate, and although thirst is a parallel response to the same stimulus, ADH itself acts on the kidney.

cards.q: A student draws the renin pathway with an arrow showing the macula densa secreting renin into the blood. Where is the error?
cards.a: The macula densa is the sensor; granular cells release the renin.
options: The macula densa is correct, but renin should act on the lung first
The macula densa is the sensor; granular cells release the renin
The macula densa releases aldosterone rather than renin
The macula densa is the effector and the granular cells the sensor
cards.explanation: Macula densa cells sit in the wall of the distal tubule where it touches its own glomerulus, sense NaCl delivery, and signal the neighboring granular cells of the afferent arteriole, which are the cells that actually release renin. The pathway does pass through the lung, but that is where ACE turns angiotensin I into angiotensin II, a later step and not a fix for the wrong source. Aldosterone comes from the adrenal cortex. Calling the macula densa an effector reverses its role in the loop.

cards.q: A calcium diagram shows plasma Ca2+ falling, PTH rising, and an arrow to the kidney labeled raises urinary calcium loss. What correction is needed?
cards.a: PTH raises renal Ca2+ reabsorption, so urinary loss falls.
options: The arrow is right, since PTH raises urinary calcium loss
PTH acts only on bone, so the renal arrow should be deleted
The stimulus is wrong, since PTH rises when plasma Ca2+ rises
PTH raises renal Ca2+ reabsorption, so urinary loss falls
cards.explanation: Every action of PTH raises plasma Ca2+, so the renal arrow must show more reabsorption and less calcium in the urine, alongside bone resorption and calcitriol driven absorption from the gut. Dumping calcium in the urine would work against the stimulus and break the negative feedback. PTH has three targets, so deleting the renal arrow leaves the diagram incomplete. A rise in plasma Ca2+ suppresses PTH rather than stimulating it.

cards.q: A student draws a homeostatic pathway as a straight line from stimulus to response with no return arrow. What can that diagram no longer show?
cards.a: That the response feeds back and shuts off the original stimulus.
options: That the sensor sends information to the integrating center
That the effector produces a measurable physiological change
That the stimulus is a change in a regulated variable
That the response feeds back and shuts off the original stimulus
cards.explanation: The closing arrow is what turns the drawing into a loop, and without it there is no way to show regulation at all, only a one way chain of events. The afferent limb from sensor to integrating center is still drawn in the straight line version. The effector and its response are also still on the page. The stimulus is still labeled too; what is missing is what the response does back to it.

cards.q: A student diagrams the response to a one liter hemorrhage and stops after increased heart rate and vasoconstriction. Which step must be added to show how blood volume itself is rebuilt over hours?
cards.a: Renin release leading to angiotensin II and aldosterone, with Na+ and water retention.
options: ANP release from the stretched atrial wall, with more Na+ and more water lost in the urine
Renin release leading to angiotensin II and aldosterone, with Na+ and water retention
A rise in glomerular filtration rate, with a larger volume of dilute urine
Withdrawal of sympathetic drive to the kidney, with renal blood flow rising
cards.explanation: The neural limb buys time by defending pressure, but volume can only be rebuilt by retaining salt and water, which is what the renin, angiotensin and aldosterone arm does, together with ADH driven water reabsorption and thirst. ANP would push volume the wrong way, and its release actually falls when the atria are underfilled. GFR drops rather than rises after hemorrhage, and dilute urine would throw away the water being conserved. Sympathetic drive to the kidney rises in hemorrhage, and that rise is part of what stimulates renin.

cards.q: In a drawing of the hypothalamic, pituitary and thyroid axis, a student makes the arrow from thyroid hormone back to the pituitary stimulatory. What would that diagram predict?
cards.a: Thyroid hormone would keep driving its own release, with no stable level.
options: Thyroid hormone would settle at a stable level slightly above normal
TSH would fall as thyroid hormone rose, just as in the real axis
Thyroid hormone would keep driving its own release, with no stable level
The hypothalamus would stop releasing TRH once the thyroid responded
cards.explanation: Making the return arrow stimulatory turns the axis into positive feedback: each rise in thyroid hormone raises TSH, which raises thyroid hormone again, and nothing ever sets a level. In the real axis thyroid hormone inhibits both TSH and TRH, and that inhibition is exactly what holds the hormone in a narrow range. Settling at a stable level, even a high one, still requires a negative return arrow. Saying TSH falls as thyroid hormone rises describes the correct diagram, not the one this student drew.

cards.q: A student's altitude diagram runs low inspired PO2, peripheral chemoreceptors, increased ventilation, then an arrow to the kidney labeled excretes bicarbonate. What annotation belongs on the arrow between ventilation and the kidney?
cards.a: PCO2 falls and arterial pH rises, and that alkalosis is what the kidney answers.
options: PCO2 falls and arterial pH rises, and that alkalosis is what the kidney answers
PCO2 rises and arterial pH falls, and that acidosis is what the kidney answers
Arterial PO2 returns to sea level values, ending the hypoxic drive
Plasma bicarbonate rises first, and the kidney then corrects it downward
cards.explanation: Hyperventilation blows off CO2, so PCO2 falls and pH rises into respiratory alkalosis, and it is that alkalosis the kidney answers by excreting HCO3- over the following day or two. If PCO2 rose and pH fell, the kidney would retain bicarbonate instead, which is the opposite renal response. Arterial PO2 does improve with hyperventilation but stays well below sea level values, which is why the hypoxic drive persists. Plasma bicarbonate does not rise first; it falls as the result of the renal step.

cards.q: A student draws the response to drinking one liter of water as falling plasma osmolarity connected straight to a large dilute urine, with nothing in between. Which element is missing, and which way does it move?
cards.a: ADH, which decreases, so the collecting duct becomes less permeable to water.
options: ADH, which decreases, so the collecting duct becomes less permeable to water
ADH, which increases, so the collecting duct becomes more permeable to water
Aldosterone, which decreases, so less Na+ is reabsorbed distally
Renin, which increases, so angiotensin II constricts the efferent arteriole
cards.explanation: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors sense the fall in osmolarity, ADH release drops, aquaporins are pulled out of the collecting duct membrane, and water stays in the tubule to make a large dilute urine. ADH increasing would concentrate the urine instead, the opposite of what the student's own endpoint shows. Aldosterone regulates Na+ balance and volume rather than the free water excretion at issue here. Renin and angiotensin II defend pressure and filtration and are not the missing link between osmolarity and urine dilution.
